nameStory: The 'blue scarlet pimpernel' gets its puzzling name from being the blue-flowered cousin of the more common scarlet (red) pimpernel. Both were once called 'pimpernel' from the Old French 'pimprenelle,' meaning a small, delicate flower that seems to wink at you as it opens and closes with the weather.
description: Blue scarlet pimpernel is a tiny, creeping annual wildflower that most people walk right past without noticing. This delicate plant stays close to the ground, rarely reaching more than 4-6 inches tall, with thin trailing stems that spread along the soil. Its small blue flowers, about the size of a pencil eraser, peek up from between small oval leaves. Despite being related to showier loosestrifes, this little plant is all about subtlety and going unnoticed.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny bright blue flowers, each about 1/4 inch across with 5 rounded petals that feel papery to the touch. The flowers open only in sunny weather and close on cloudy days or in late afternoon, giving them a 'now you see me, now you don't' quality.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small oval leaves, about 1/2 inch long, arranged in pairs along the stem (opposite). The leaves feel smooth and slightly succulent, with a fresh, mild scent when gently crushed between your fingers.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing and sprawling, with thin, weak stems that trail along the ground rather than standing upright. The whole plant has a delicate, almost fragile appearance that seems to hug whatever surface it's growing on.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces tiny round capsules that split open like a miniature hinged box, releasing dust-like seeds. The capsules are so small you might need to look closely to spot them tucked behind where the flowers were.

habitat: This extremely rare plant in New England prefers sandy, disturbed soils in coastal areas, vacant lots, and waste places. It thrives in spots that are sunny but not too rich in nutrients, often appearing in thin soil between pavement cracks or along sandy roadsides. Given its rarity here (only 2 recorded observations), it's likely found mostly near ports or developed areas where it might have been accidentally introduced.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate as soil warms, with tiny seedlings appearing in late spring. Young plants are almost microscopic and easily overlooked.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering occurs from June through August, when the tiny blue flowers open during sunny morning hours. This is the best time to spot this elusive plant.
seasonality.fall: Plants continue flowering into early fall, then set seed in small capsules. The entire plant dies back as an annual after releasing its dust-like seeds.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground presence - exists only as seeds waiting in the soil for next year's growing season.

funFact: This tiny flower is like a natural weather station - it opens its petals only when atmospheric pressure is high and humidity is low, actually closing up hours before rain arrives, earning it the folk name 'poor man's weather glass.'
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with its red-flowered cousin, scarlet pimpernel, which has identical leaves and growth habit but orange-red flowers. Remember: 'Blue blooms, same rooms' - they often grow in similar disturbed habitats, but the flower color is the giveaway.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name including 'scarlet,' this plant is actually blue-flowered - the name comes from it being in the same species complex as the red scarlet pimpernel. Both plants were historically used in folk medicine and were believed to have magical properties for treating eye ailments, though neither should be used medicinally today.
compareHints: Unlike other Lysimachia species in New England that tend to be taller perennials with yellow flowers (like whorled loosestrife or swamp candles), blue scarlet pimpernel is a tiny blue-flowered annual that creeps along the ground. It's much smaller and more delicate than its loosestrife cousins, lacking their upright growth and showy flower clusters.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its loosestrife relatives that tend to be taller with yellow flowers and different leaf arrangements, northern starflower is much shorter with its distinctive white seven-petaled blooms and single whorl of leaves.
Among New England's many Lysimachia species, whorled loosestrife is instantly recognizable by its four-leaf whorls - no other loosestrife has this arrangement.
Among its loosestrife relatives, swamp candles is unique for its tall, narrow flower spike - most other Lysimachia species have flowers in leaf axils or shorter, broader clusters.
Among New England's loosestrifes, fringed loosestrife is distinctive for its opposite leaves with fringed leaf stems and nodding yellow flowers.
Among its loosestrife relatives in New England, creeping Jenny is unique for its trailing, mat-forming habit - most other Lysimachia species stand upright.
Dotted loosestrife stands out from its loosestrife cousins mainly by those telltale petal spots - no other Lysimachia species has them.
Unlike its loosestrife cousins in the same genus, scarlet pimpernel stays ground-hugging rather than growing upright, and its flowers are much smaller but more intensely colored.
Among the loosestrife family in New England, gooseneck loosestrife is the only one with the distinctive curved white flower spikes.
Unlike its loosestrife relatives that are mostly freshwater plants with showy yellow or white flowers, sea milkwort is the oddball of the family - adapted for salt water and lacking petals entirely.

Yellow loosestrife stands out from its loosestrife relatives by its tall stature and dense yellow flower clusters - most other Lysimachia species in New England are shorter with more scattered flowers.
Among its loosestrife cousins, tufted loosestrife is unique for having flowers that emerge from the sides of the stem rather than at the tips.

Among New England's yellow-flowered loosestrifes, lowland loosestrife is distinguished by its flowers tucked into leaf axils rather than arranged in showy spikes like swamp candles, or whorled around the stem like whorled loosestrife.
Among its loosestrife relatives, lanceleaf loosestrife is distinguished by its alternate (not opposite or whorled) leaf arrangement and narrow, lance-shaped leaves.
Unlike its flashy cousin creeping Jenny (regular moneywort), miniature moneywort is truly miniature in every way - much smaller leaves, tinier flowers, and more delicate growth.
